chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa from Ali ibn al-Hakam from Yahya ibn Mihran from Abdullah ibn al-Hasan said:

I asked him about the qaramil. He said, 'And what is the qaramil?' I said, 'Wool that women place on their heads.' He said, 'If it is wool, there is no harm with it, but if it is hair, there is no good in it like the wasilah (hairpiece) of the wasilah (one who attaches hair) and the mawsulah (one who is attached with hair).'

key_terms.الْقَرَامِلِ: Plural of qaramil, referring to hairpieces or wigs
key_terms.الْمَوْصُولَةِ: The one who is attached (with hair), referring to the wearer or the attached hair
key_terms.الْوَاصِلَةِ: The one who attaches (hair), referring to a hairpiece or the act of attaching
key_terms.شَعْرًا: Hair (specifically human hair in this context)

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic ruling on women wearing human hair extensions or wigs according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, the Imam clarifies the permissibility of the *qaramil* (hairpiece) by distinguishing its material composition, permitting wool while criting human hair. The comparison to the *wasilah* (one who connects hair) suggests that human hairpieces may carry the same ritual impurity (*najis*) status as the hair of the deceased, reflecting the Shia juristic view on the purity of bodily remains. This distinction highlights the importance of material origin in determining the ritual status of adornments in Shia fiqh.
